Update 5/18/2026 As a one-time benefit to suppliers who have successfully qualified for exemption from prior authorization, CMS is extending the supplier opt-out period for an additional week, beginning May 18, 2026, through May 26, 2026. Any opt-out request received after close of business on May 26, 2026, will be denied, and those suppliers will be exempt from prior authorization starting June 1, 2026. Please contact your DME MAC or visit your DME MAC’s website for more information. Update 1/13/2026 The Prior Authorization Exemption Process On December 2, 2025, CMS issued CMS-1828-F, which establishes a prior authorization exemption process for certain DMEPOS items. This process permits DMEPOS suppliers that demonstrate billing compliance with Medicare coverage, coding, and payment requirements to be exempt from required prior authorization. Suppliers who achieve a provisional affirmation rate of 90% or higher may qualify for exemption. Suppliers will have the option to opt out of the exemption. Should suppliers no longer meet the exemption criteria, a notice of withdrawal will be provided at least 60 days before the effective date. Suppliers will receive notice from the DME MAC of their exemption status no later than April 2, 2026. The first exemption cycle will begin on June 1, 2026, and will run annually thereafter. For more information, please see the updated Operational Guide (PDF) and FAQs (PDF). Updates to the Master List and the Required Prior Authorization List CMS announced in the Federal Register on 1/13/2026 updates to the Master List and the Required Prior Authorization List. The Master List update includes the addition of 18 HCPCS codes effective 4/13/2026. The Required Prior Authorization List update includes the selection of seven HCPCS codes. The additional selections include certain orthoses and pneumatic compression device items. Prior authorization as a condition of payment begins nationwide 4/13/2026 for the newly added codes. The review timeframe for expedited requests will remain 2 business days. The Required Prior Authorization List update includes the selection of nine HCPCS codes. The additional selections include certain lower limb orthoses, lumbar sacral orthoses, and osteogenesis stimulators. Prior authorization as a condition of payment begins nationwide 08/12/2024 for the newly added LLO and LSO codes. Prior authorization as a condition of payment for the osteogenesis stimulator codes is completed in two phases. A complete prior authorization submission should include a combination of required documentation, medical-justification information, and payer-specific evidence. The evidence provided shows that prior authorization is not merely a formality; it is a process designed to confirm medical necessity before payment, and missing documentation can lead to denial or delays [N2-R5][N4-F2].

## 1) Which specific documents or forms are required
The evidence indicates that prior authorization requests typically require documentation to support the medical need, but the exact form can vary by payer. The CMS DMEPOS prior authorization guidance describes the process for certain durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS), and Noridian Medicare specifically notes that prior authorization submissions for orthoses must be completed through its designated process [N4-F2][N4-F3]. However, the search results do not provide a single universal form, so the safest conclusion is that the submission should include:

- A completed prior authorization request form or template provided by the payer or carrier [N4-F2][N4-F3]
- Any required attachments or supporting clinical documentation
- Identification of the HCPCS code and the item being requested [N4-F2]
- Information on how the item will be supplied or billed [N4-F2]

The UHC guidance also emphasizes that UnitedHealthcare Community Plan may require a written prescription from the ordering provider, and if the ordering provider is also the supplier, office visit notes are required. When such documentation is not submitted, code L3000 will deny [N1-F1]. This implies that for some payers, even a request without the proper form or attached evidence can be rejected.

## 2) What medical necessity or justification must be provided
The evidence shows that prior authorization is used to confirm that care is necessary before payment, and the justification should be tied to the patient’s condition and the clinical benefit of the item. The CMS guidance explains that the prior authorization process is for “certain DMEPOS” items with high rates of unnecessary utilization [N4-F2]. Noridian Medicare similarly describes the program as targeting orthotic HCPCS codes that historically demonstrate high unnecessary utilization [N4-F3]. That suggests the required justification should demonstrate:

- A clear medical indication for the orthotic
- Why the item is appropriate for the patient’s condition
- That the item is needed rather than being used unnecessarily
- That the item is appropriate for the patient’s foot or lower-extremity issue

The Harvard Health article also notes that prior authorization is used to confirm that care is necessary before payment [N5-R5]. That means the submission should not simply state that the item is requested; it should explain why it is medically appropriate.

## 3) Whether a diagnosis, exam note, or other evidence is mandatory
The evidence supports a “yes” answer, but with nuance. The UHC guidance is explicit: for L3000 orthotics, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan will reimburse L3000 only when accompanied by a written prescription from the provider ordering the orthotic, unless the ordering provider is also the supplier. When the ordering provider is also the supplier, office visit notes are required. When such documentation is not submitted, code L3000 will deny [N1-F1]. This means the documentation is mandatory for L3000 under UHC, not merely recommended.

The broader CMS/DMEPOS guidance also suggests that medical review can be part of the prior authorization process [N4-F2]. That implies that payers may require some form of clinical evidence, even if they do not explicitly require a full exam note in every case. The search results also indicate that prior authorization requests should include indication, prior failed therapies, and clinical support [N2-R3], which reinforces that justification is mandatory rather than optional.

## 4) What happens if documentation is missing
The evidence is clear that missing documentation can result in denial. The UHC guidance states that when documentation is not submitted, code L3000 will deny [N1-F1]. Noridian Medicare’s guidance similarly implies that incomplete submissions are likely to be rejected, since it frames prior authorization as a process requiring documentation [N4-F3]. The Harvard Health article also explains that prior authorization is a tool insurers use to confirm care is necessary before paying, which means payers will often deny claims if they cannot verify medical need [N5-R5].

In practice, missing documentation can also delay processing, because payers may request additional information before making a decision [N2-R5]. The evidence does not specify a universal penalty for missing documentation, but it does show that the absence of required evidence is a strong signal for denial [N1-F1][N2-R5].

## Bottom line
A complete prior authorization submission should include:
- A completed request form or template [N4-F2][N4-F3]
- A written prescription or equivalent provider documentation [N1-F1]
- Office visit notes, if the provider is also the supplier [N1-F1]
- Clinical justification showing medical necessity [N2-R3][N5-R5]
- Any other required attachments or supporting evidence [N4-F2]

If any of these are missing, especially the prescription or visit notes for L3000, the submission is likely to be denied or delayed [N1-F1][N2-R5].
